name: French Defense, MacCutcheon Variation
summary: The MacCutcheon Variation is a combative French where Black answers 4.Bg5 with 4...Bb4, pinning the knight instead of playing the quiet Be7.
intro: In the MacCutcheon, Black meets the Classical French sequence 1.e4 e6 2.d4 d5 3.Nc3 Nf6 4.Bg5 not with the solid 4...Be7 but with 4...Bb4, pinning the c3-knight and generating immediate central tension and sharp, imbalanced play.
line: e4 e6 d4 d5 Nc3 Nf6 Bg5 Bb4

sections.heading: Strategic ideas
paragraphs: By pinning the knight, Black challenges White's grip on e4 and dares White to resolve the tension in the centre. The typical follow-up 5.e5 h6 6.Bd2 Bxc3 7.bxc3 Ne4 hands White the bishop pair and a broad centre but saddles White with doubled c-pawns, while Black's kingside is slightly loosened by ...h6.

The resulting middlegames are richly imbalanced: White has more space and open lines for the bishops, whereas Black counts on the structural weakness of the doubled pawns and active piece play, often with a knight anchored on e4 and pressure against the c-pawns and d4.

sections.heading: Main variations
paragraphs: The main line runs 5.e5 h6 6.Bd2, when Black continues 6...Bxc3 7.bxc3 Ne4, occupying the strong central square and forcing White to prove the value of the bishop pair and space. Play frequently revolves around White's kingside ambitions versus Black's queenside targets.

White has independent tries in 6.Be3, keeping the dark-squared bishop, and the sharp 6.exf6, damaging Black's structure at the cost of the centre. Each choice steers the game into different but equally combative territory.

sections.heading: History and background
paragraphs: The variation is named after the American amateur Milton MacCutcheon, who employed it in the late nineteenth century. It has long been a respected fighting alternative in the Classical French, favoured by players who want to unbalance the game early rather than defend the more restrained 4...Be7 lines.
